title: US Announces Global Visa Restrictions Targeting Cybercriminals and Sextortion Networks
excerpt: Secretary of State Marco Rubio unveils new policy under the Immigration and Nationality Act, warning that the US 'will go after those who prey on our citizens.'
body:
• US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a new visa restriction policy targeting individuals involved in cybercrime and cyber-enabled crimes such as sextortion.
  • The policy extends to immediate family members of those complicit in criminal enterprises.
  • Rubio cited Chinese transnational criminal organisations that defrauded US citizens of at least $10 billion in 2024 alone.
  • The announcement is part of a broader administration strategy deploying sanctions, prosecutions, and international cooperation against criminal networks.

The United States on Thursday unveiled a new global visa restriction policy targeting foreign nationals involved in cybercrime and cyber-enabled crime, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio warning that Washington "will go after those who prey on our citizens."

Scope of the New Policy

The restrictions, implemented under the Immigration and Nationality Act, cover individuals responsible for or complicit in cyberscams and sextortion schemes, according to a statement from the US State Department. Rubio confirmed that the policy would also extend to certain immediate family members of those engaged in such criminal activities, according to Reuters.

"By restricting visa issuance to those who are responsible for or complicit in these criminal enterprises, we are sending a clear message: The United States will go after those who prey on our citizens."

— Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State

The policy targets a range of cyber-enabled crimes, from online investment scams to sextortion operations that specifically target American minors. Rubio described sextortion as "devastating families and futures" and singled out overseas criminal operations that exploit children.

$10 Billion in Losses

Rubio pointed to the scale of the problem, noting that scammers "often orchestrated by Chinese transnational criminal organizations" defrauded US citizens of at least $10 billion in 2024 alone, according to administration estimates. These operations also fuel corruption, money laundering, and human trafficking, the secretary said.

The Trump administration has taken a multi-pronged approach to combating these networks. Rubio said the government is "deploying every tool at our disposal — sanctions, prosecutions, asset seizures, extradition requests, and international law enforcement cooperation — to dismantle criminal scam networks and impose costs on those who enable them."

Part of a Broader Immigration Crackdown

The cybercrime visa restrictions are part of a wider pattern of immigration enforcement actions by the Trump administration. Earlier this month, the State Department announced visa restrictions targeting members of far-left and aligned groups accused of using violence, including bombings and intimidation, to pursue political objectives.

The measures align with the National Security Presidential Memorandum-7, which aims to prevent foreign nationals linked with violent and criminal activities from entering the US, according to Devdiscourse.

The administration has also recently finalised sweeping changes to the nonimmigrant visa system, replacing the decades-old "duration of status" policy with fixed admission periods for international students on F-1 visas (capped at four years), exchange visitors on J-1 visas, and foreign journalists on I visas. That rule, scheduled to take effect September 15, has drawn sharp criticism from universities, press freedom advocates, and foreign governments — including India, which said it is monitoring the situation.

What It Means for the Diaspora

While the cybercrime visa restrictions target criminal networks rather than lawful immigrants, the policy adds to a rapidly shifting immigration landscape that Indian nationals must navigate. The administration's simultaneous actions on student visas, journalist visas, and now cybercrime-related restrictions signal a broad tightening of the US visa regime. Indian professionals and families — among the largest groups of US visa applicants globally — face increasing scrutiny and uncertainty as these layered enforcement measures take shape.

India's Ministry of External Affairs has said it remains in contact with Washington to safeguard the interests of Indian citizens affected by the various policy changes.
nri_angle: The new visa restriction policy adds another layer to the US immigration enforcement framework that Indian professionals and families navigate, and comes amid a broader crackdown that has already targeted student and work visas.
